First listed 2025-05-05 · episode or wrap

Navigating the Storm: US–China Tariffs' Impact on Logistics

Fuller maps the tariff shock from Chinese orders through ports, trucking, inventories and retail. Eisman probes denominators and challenges exaggerated claims that partial disruptions mean a complete stop. The interview distinguishes immediate freight-sector pain from later shortages, but its near-zero probability of a quick China agreement failed within twelve days. Conditional shortage and earnings scenarios require more care because policy changed. Fuller's extreme domestic-food share and net-food-exporter premises conflict with official data, while the proprietary freight statistics remain unverified.

YouTube · 2025-05-05 ↗
Useful operational transmission analysis and explicit scope challenges coexist with a failed near-term political forecast and weakly verified freight extrapolations. Guest claims are kept separate from Eisman's scorecard.

Source version, speaker attribution and transcript cautions

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

YouTube automatic captions; speaker attribution requires context

The normalized transcript names Steve Eisman and Craig Fuller inline throughout; dialogue confirms questions versus answers. Guest assertions are not treated as Eisman endorsements merely because he repeats them for clarification.

  • Recorded April 30, 2025 after the market close; published May 5.
  • The opening montage repeats the order-pause discussion; substantive timestamps are used.
  • Bookings, actual shipments, containers and baseline versus year-over-year changes are sometimes conflated.
  • The 450,000-500,000 jobs example moves from all logistics to trucking alone.
  • Food share has no calorie or tonnage denominator; the audit uses FDA supply and USDA spending evidence explicitly.
  • The J.B. Hunt call/tariff chronology is recalled uncertainly and is incorrect.

Conditional reasoning

For price P and imported cost C=(1-g)P, with g=.30 to .40, duty 1.45C=.87P to 1.015P exceeds original gross profit .30P to .40P. This requires customs value to equal the assumed imported cost and no offsetting adjustment.

Assessment test: Verify customs value and retail-cost relationships for actual products.

  • Separate import-accounting effects, survey sentiment and measured activity.
  • Keep the no-agreement counterfactual separate from an explicit probability forecast.
  • Check denominator consistency when moving from logistics jobs to trucking jobs.
